name: RBS Calculator
use_case: Design and predict RBS sequences for target expression levels
description: Predicts translation initiation rates from RBS and coding sequences. Most widely cited tool in iGEM for tuning protein expression in bacteria.
how_to_use: Paste your coding sequence start region into the calculator. Set your target translation initiation rate (start with 10,000 au for moderate expression). The tool outputs an optimized RBS sequence you can order directly from IDT. iGEM teams use this to fine-tune expression of reporter genes and enzymes before cloning.

name: Benchling
description: Cloud platform for sequence design primer design codon optimization and lab notebook. Free for academic users. Official iGEM sponsor. Used by majority of iGEM teams.
output: Annotated plasmid maps / primers / lab records
how_to_use: Sign up with your university email for free academic access. Create a project folder for your team. Design plasmids using the sequence editor — annotate features drag and drop parts and use the built-in primer designer. Store all protocols and results in the lab notebook. Share access with all team members so everyone sees the same version of constructs.

name: SnapGene
description: Desktop tool for plasmid visualization Gibson/Golden Gate simulation and Sanger alignment. Wizard-driven cloning design with automatic primer suggestions. Free viewer available.
how_to_use: Download the free Viewer to open .dna files or use the full version (free for iGEM). Import your vector sequence and insert. Use the Cloning Wizard to simulate Gibson Assembly — it automatically designs primers with correct overlaps and checks the final construct. Verify your Sanger sequencing results by aligning reads to your plasmid map.

name: ApE (A Plasmid Editor)
use_case: Free plasmid editing and cloning simulation
description: Free desktop plasmid editor with built-in simulators for PCR Gibson restriction-ligation and Golden Gate assembly. No installation required on Mac.
how_to_use: Download and open ApE. Paste your sequence or open a GenBank file. Use Enzyme → Single Cutters to find restriction sites for analytical digests. For Gibson Assembly use the In-Silico PCR function to simulate your amplicons. Color-code your annotations by feature type for easy visualization in lab meetings.

name: NEBuilder
description: NEB's official Gibson Assembly design tool. Designs primers with correct overlaps for any combination of fragments automatically.
how_to_use: Go to the NEBuilder website and create a new assembly. Paste in your vector sequence (linearized) and each insert sequence. Set the overlap length (20 bp default works well). The tool outputs primer sequences for each fragment — order these from IDT or Sigma. Always verify the assembled sequence in SnapGene before ordering.

name: NEBCutter
description: Finds all restriction enzyme cut sites in a DNA sequence. Essential for restriction cloning and analytical digest planning.
how_to_use: Paste your plasmid sequence and select which enzyme sets to search (NEB recommends checking all commercial enzymes). Filter for enzymes that cut once in your insert and zero times in your backbone. Use the results to plan your restriction cloning strategy or design analytical digest patterns to verify correct cloning.

name: COPASI
use_case: ODE-based modeling of genetic circuits and biochemical networks
description: Most widely used modeling tool in iGEM. Models promoter dynamics protein production and degradation as systems of ODEs. Graphical interface no coding required.
how_to_use: Download COPASI and create a new model. Add species (proteins mRNAs) and reactions (transcription translation degradation). Enter rate constants from literature — start with typical E. coli parameters (mRNA half-life ~2 min protein half-life ~60 min). Run a time-course simulation to predict steady-state expression. Compare to your experimental fluorescence data to validate the model.

name: MATLAB
description: Commercial software offered free to iGEM teams. Used for ODE modeling signal processing and data fitting. Simulink extension for block-diagram circuit modeling.
how_to_use: Apply for free MATLAB access through iGEM's partnership. Use the ode45 solver to numerically integrate your ODE system. The Curve Fitting Toolbox helps extract kinetic parameters from experimental data. Simulink is useful for modeling feedback circuits visually. Export figures directly for your wiki.

name: Tellurium
description: Python library for SBML-based modeling of biological networks. Combines roadrunner simulation engine with Antimony model description language.
how_to_use: Install via pip: pip install tellurium. Write your model in Antimony notation (similar to chemical equations). Run simulations with r.simulate() and plot with matplotlib. Tellurium is ideal if your team already uses Python — integrates with Jupyter notebooks for reproducible modeling pages on your wiki.

name: AlphaFold
description: DeepMind's revolutionary structure prediction tool. Predicts 3D protein structures from amino acid sequence with near-experimental accuracy. Database of 200M+ predicted structures.
how_to_use: Search the AlphaFold database first — your protein may already have a prediction. For novel sequences use ColabFold (colab.research.google.com) for free GPU-accelerated prediction. Download the PDB file and open in PyMOL to visualize binding sites. Check the pLDDT confidence score — regions above 70 are reliable for structural interpretation.

name: ESMFold
description: Meta's protein language model for fast structure prediction. Useful for rapid screening of multiple variants. API available.
how_to_use: Use the ESMFold web server to quickly predict structures for multiple protein variants without waiting for AlphaFold. Paste up to 400 amino acids and get a structure in seconds. Compare variant structures to identify mutations that affect the binding pocket or stability. ESMFold is faster than AlphaFold — ideal for screening libraries.

name: PyMOL
description: Industry-standard tool for visualizing and analyzing protein structures. Used in iGEM to present structural results and design binding interfaces. Educational license free.
how_to_use: Apply for a free educational license at pymol.org/edu. Load your PDB file with File → Open. Use the Show menu to switch between cartoon ribbon and surface representations. Color by chain or by B-factor/pLDDT. For figures use Ray → Ray to render high-quality images for your wiki. Use the Measurement Wizard to calculate distances between residues.

name: CRISPOR
use_case: Guide RNA design and off-target scoring
description: Designs guide RNAs for any CRISPR system and scores off-target sites. Supports 100+ genomes and multiple Cas proteins.
how_to_use: Paste your target DNA sequence (200 bp around the cut site) and select your organism and Cas protein. CRISPOR outputs all possible guide RNAs ranked by efficiency score and off-target risk. Select guides with high on-target score (>50) and low off-target score. Order the top 3 guides and test all in parallel — efficiency varies in practice.

name: Cas-OFFinder
description: Fast algorithm for finding all potential off-target sites for a given guide RNA. Essential for validating CRISPR specificity.
how_to_use: Enter your guide RNA sequence and PAM and select your target genome. Set the mismatch threshold (2-3 mismatches is standard for validation). Download the results and check whether off-target sites are in coding regions or regulatory elements. Run this before committing to a guide sequence — finding off-targets early saves weeks.

name: IDT OligoAnalyzer
use_case: Primer Tm and secondary structure analysis
description: Analyzes primer melting temperature hairpin formation and dimer formation. Used to validate primers before ordering.
how_to_use: Paste each primer sequence into OligoAnalyzer and set your PCR conditions (salt concentration and oligo concentration). Check that Tm is within 2°C of your other primer. Look at the hairpin and dimer ΔG values — anything more negative than -9 kcal/mol may cause problems. Redesign primers with strong self-complementarity before ordering.

name: Primer3
description: Classic primer design tool. Designs primers for PCR sequencing and hybridization with full control over Tm GC content and amplicon size.
how_to_use: Paste your template sequence and mark the region to amplify with brackets []. Set product size range (typically 500-1000 bp for colony PCR) and Tm range (58-62°C). Primer3 outputs multiple primer pairs ranked by quality. Always check candidates in OligoAnalyzer before ordering and BLAST them against your organism's genome to check for off-target binding.

name: NCBI BLAST
description: Searches sequence databases to find homologous sequences. Essential for verifying part sequences confirming gene identity and finding related proteins.
how_to_use: Use BLASTn for DNA sequences and BLASTp for proteins. After receiving your synthesized gene BLAST it against the nr database to confirm identity. For finding homologs of your target enzyme use BLASTp to identify candidates from other organisms with potentially better properties. Filter results by percent identity and coverage.

name: Clustal Omega
description: Aligns multiple DNA or protein sequences to identify conserved regions. Used in iGEM for comparing promoter variants or protein homologs.
how_to_use: Paste multiple sequences in FASTA format and run the alignment. Conserved residues appear as asterisks below the alignment — these are usually functionally critical. Use the alignment to identify which positions to mutate for directed evolution. Export as ClustalW format and open in Jalview for color-coded visualization.

name: SWISS-MODEL
description: Automated homology modeling server. Builds 3D protein models based on known template structures. Widely used when AlphaFold confidence is low.
how_to_use: Go to the SWISS-MODEL server and paste your protein sequence. The server automatically finds the best template structure and builds a model. Check the QMEAN score — values above -4 indicate a reliable model. Download the PDB file and open in PyMOL. Use the model to guide mutagenesis experiments by identifying active site residues.

name: Rosetta
description: Suite of algorithms for protein structure prediction design and modeling. Used in iGEM for enzyme design and protein engineering.
how_to_use: Apply for a free academic license. Use the RosettaCommons tutorials to get started. For most iGEM applications PyRosetta (Python interface) is easiest — install via pip. Use the FastRelax protocol to optimize a protein structure after mutation. The InterfaceAnalyzer app evaluates binding affinity changes from mutations.

name: iGEM Parts Registry
description: Central repository of standard biological parts used in iGEM. Contains promoters RBS coding sequences and terminators with characterization data.
how_to_use: Search by function (e.g. 'GFP reporter') or browse by category. Check the Experience tab for each part — this shows results from other teams who used it. Prefer parts with 'Works' experience ratings and multiple data points. Download sequences as FASTA or GenBank. Always verify your received part by sequencing before using in experiments.

name: SynBioHub
description: Open-source repository for synthetic biology designs. Stores and shares genetic designs in SBOL format. Integrated with Benchling and other tools.
how_to_use: Search SynBioHub for your gene of interest or part. Download designs as SBOL2 or FASTA. Use the SynBioHub plugin in Benchling to import parts directly into your design environment. When depositing your own parts create a collection for your team and add all characterized parts with their sequence and experimental data.

name: Addgene
description: Non-profit plasmid repository. Teams deposit and share plasmids. Extensive protocol library for standard molecular biology techniques.
how_to_use: Search for your backbone vector (e.g. pUC19 pET28a) by name. Request plasmids directly from Addgene — delivery takes 1-2 weeks so order early. Read the depositing lab's protocol in the plasmid page notes. After your project deposit your characterized plasmids so future teams can build on your work.

name: iBioSim
description: Tool for modeling and simulation of genetic circuits using SBML. Integrates design verification and simulation in one environment.
how_to_use: Download iBioSim from GitHub. Use the SBOL Canvas integration to draw your genetic circuit graphically. Convert the design to an SBML model automatically. Run stochastic simulations to model cell-to-cell variability in expression — important for toggle switches and oscillators. Export simulation results as CSV for plotting.

name: BOOST
description: JBEI tool for codon optimization reverse translation and sequence verification against synthesis constraints like GC content and repeats.
how_to_use: Go to the BOOST web server and paste your protein sequence. Select your host organism for codon optimization. Set constraints for GC content (40-60%) and repeat removal to ensure the sequence can be synthesized without errors. Download the optimized DNA sequence and verify it in SnapGene before submitting to your synthesis provider.

name: Geneious Prime
description: Full-featured bioinformatics platform for sequence assembly alignment annotation and analysis. Offered free to iGEM teams alongside SnapGene.
how_to_use: Apply for free iGEM access. Import your Sanger sequencing .ab1 files directly. Use the De Novo Assembly function to assemble reads and check coverage. The built-in annotation tools automatically identify ORFs promoters and restriction sites. Build phylogenetic trees from multiple sequence alignments to show evolutionary context of your target gene.

name: WebLogo
description: Creates sequence logo diagrams showing conservation at each position in an alignment. Used to visualize promoter and RBS conservation.
how_to_use: Run your multiple sequence alignment in Clustal Omega first. Paste the alignment output into WebLogo. Adjust the output format (PNG PDF) and size for your wiki. Sequence logos clearly show which positions are conserved (tall letters) versus variable (short letters) — use this to identify key residues in your promoter or protein.

name: protocols.io
description: Platform for writing sharing and versioning wet-lab protocols. Many iGEM teams publish their protocols here. DOI-citable.
how_to_use: Create a free account and search for existing protocols before writing your own — many standard procedures (Gibson Assembly miniprep transformation) are already there. When writing new protocols use the step-by-step editor with materials list. Publish your protocol to get a DOI — this satisfies iGEM's documentation requirements and lets other teams cite your methods.

name: FPbase
description: Database of fluorescent protein properties including excitation/emission spectra brightness and photostability. Essential for choosing reporters.
how_to_use: Search FPbase for fluorescent proteins compatible with your microscope filter sets. Use the Spectra Viewer to check for spectral overlap between multiple FPs if doing co-localization experiments. Compare brightness (EC × QY) and photostability values when choosing between variants. mNeonGreen and mScarlet are current favorites for high brightness.

name: Non-Repetitive Parts Calculator
description: Salis Lab tool for designing libraries of non-repetitive promoters RBS and other regulatory elements to avoid recombination.
how_to_use: Use this when building circuits with multiple copies of similar elements — e.g. multiple T7 promoters or Anderson promoters that could recombine. Input your target expression levels for each part. The calculator outputs sequences that are functionally equivalent but have low sequence similarity preventing recombination. Essential for multi-gene circuits.

name: MUSCLE
description: Fast and accurate multiple sequence alignment algorithm. Alternative to Clustal for large datasets.
how_to_use: Use MUSCLE when aligning more than 50 sequences — it's faster than Clustal Omega at scale. Submit sequences in FASTA format through the EBI server. The output alignment can be imported into Jalview or used directly in WebLogo. For phylogenetic analysis in iGEM projects MUSCLE alignments feed into IQ-TREE for maximum likelihood trees.

name: I-TASSER
description: Server for automated protein structure prediction and functional annotation. Consistently top-ranked in CASP competitions.
how_to_use: Submit your sequence to the I-TASSER server (registration required — free for academic). Results arrive by email in 1-5 days depending on server load. I-TASSER predicts both structure and likely function by threading against known protein families. The C-score confidence metric ranges from -5 to 2 — higher is better. Use I-TASSER when you need function prediction alongside structure.

name: CRISPRscan
description: Predicts guide RNA efficiency using machine learning model trained on in vivo data. Used to rank guides before experimental validation.
how_to_use: Enter your target gene sequence and select your organism and Cas9 variant. CRISPRscan outputs guides ranked by predicted cutting efficiency. Select top-ranked guides that also have low off-target scores from CRISPOR. Order 3 guides per target and validate by T7E1 assay or sequencing. High CRISPRscan score correlates with high in vivo efficiency.

name: Opentrons
use_case: Liquid handling automation for wet lab protocols
description: Open-source liquid handling robot widely used in iGEM for automating repetitive pipetting tasks. Protocol software is Python-based and free.
how_to_use: Write your protocol in Python using the Opentrons API (pip install opentrons). Simulate first on your computer to check for errors. Load your deck layout (tip boxes reagent tubes plates) and run on the robot. Common iGEM applications: automated transformation plating colony picking and serial dilutions. The protocol simulator catches errors before you run on actual samples.

name: ImageJ / FIJI
description: Free open-source image analysis platform. Standard tool for quantifying fluorescence microscopy images in iGEM projects.
how_to_use: Download FIJI (the ImageJ distribution with plugins). For fluorescence quantification use Analyze → Measure after setting a threshold. Use the Cell Counter plugin to count colonies or cells. For time-lapse data use the TrackMate plugin. Always subtract background fluorescence from a non-fluorescent control. Export data as CSV for plotting in Python or R.

name: FlowJo
description: Industry-standard flow cytometry analysis software. Used to quantify GFP/RFP expression at single-cell level in iGEM biosensor projects.
how_to_use: Open your FCS files in FlowJo. Create a gate hierarchy: scatter plot (FSC/SSC) to select live cells then fluorescence gate to separate positive from negative populations. Calculate the geometric mean fluorescence intensity (gMFI) for your reporter — this is more accurate than arithmetic mean for log-distributed data. Export statistics as CSV.

name: CellProfiler
description: Free open-source platform for automated analysis of biological images. Quantifies cell morphology fluorescence and phenotypic features.
how_to_use: Download CellProfiler and build a pipeline using the module drag-and-drop interface. Start with IdentifyPrimaryObjects to segment cells then MeasureObjectIntensity for fluorescence. Run on a batch of images for high-throughput analysis. CellProfiler excels at measuring subtle phenotype differences between conditions — useful for characterizing biosensor dose-response.

name: FastQC
description: Standard quality control tool for next-generation sequencing data. Run before any NGS analysis pipeline.
how_to_use: Run FastQC on your raw FASTQ files before any other analysis. The HTML report shows per-base quality scores adapter content and GC distribution. Flag files with per-base quality below 28 — these need trimming with Trimmomatic before assembly. Check the adapter content plot to confirm your sequencing library was correctly prepared.

name: SPAdes
description: Best-in-class de novo assembler for bacterial genomes and plasmids. Specifically includes a plasmid assembly mode.
how_to_use: Install SPAdes via conda (conda install -c bioconda spades). For plasmid sequencing use the --plasmid flag: spades.py --plasmid -1 R1.fastq -2 R2.fastq -o output. The assembled contigs.fasta contains your plasmid sequence. Align back to your expected construct in Geneious to verify complete assembly and check for unexpected insertions.

name: COBRApy
description: Python library for flux balance analysis of metabolic networks. Used for metabolic engineering predictions in iGEM projects.
how_to_use: Install via pip: pip install cobra. Load a genome-scale model for your organism (BiGG database has E. coli iJO1366 and yeast models). Use model.optimize() to calculate growth rate. Knock out genes with model.genes.get_by_id('b0001').knock_out() to simulate deletions. Use flux variability analysis to identify reactions essential for your target metabolite production.

name: ProteinMPNN
description: Deep learning tool for designing protein sequences that fold into a target structure. State-of-the-art for computational protein design.
how_to_use: Run ProteinMPNN through the ColabDesign notebook on Google Colab — no local installation needed. Input your target backbone structure and specify which residues to design versus fix. Generate 100+ sequences and filter by predicted confidence. Use AlphaFold2 to validate that top candidates fold back to your target structure before synthesis.

name: RFdiffusion
description: Diffusion model for de novo protein backbone generation. Enables design of novel protein structures not found in nature.
how_to_use: Access via the RFdiffusion ColabFold notebook. Specify your design goals (binding protein binder scaffold). Run the diffusion model to generate diverse backbone structures. Pass outputs through ProteinMPNN to design sequences then validate with AlphaFold2. This pipeline enables iGEM teams to design novel binders without template structures.

name: DiffDock
description: State-of-the-art diffusion-based docking tool. Predicts binding pose of small molecules to proteins.
how_to_use: Run DiffDock through the Google Colab notebook. Input your protein PDB and ligand SMILES string. DiffDock generates multiple binding pose predictions with confidence scores. Use the top-ranked pose to guide mutagenesis of binding residues. Compare predicted binding affinity with experimental measurements to validate your biosensor design.

name: Zotero
description: Free open-source reference manager. Essential for organizing literature and generating citations for iGEM wikis and papers.
how_to_use: Install Zotero desktop and the browser extension. Click the extension button on any paper page to save it automatically with all metadata. Organize papers into collections by topic. Use the Cite feature to export references in any format. For iGEM wikis export as Chicago author-date format. Share your library with teammates using Zotero Groups.

name: Jupyter Notebook
use_case: Interactive Python environment for data analysis
description: Browser-based interactive coding environment. Standard platform for reproducible data analysis and visualization in iGEM.
how_to_use: Install via pip: pip install jupyter then run jupyter notebook in your project folder. Create notebooks for each analysis (growth curves fluorescence data modeling). Use matplotlib and seaborn for publication-quality plots. Save notebooks in your GitHub repo so judges can see your exact analysis. nbviewer.jupyter.org renders notebooks directly from GitHub.

name: Biopython
description: Comprehensive Python library for biological sequence analysis. Enables programmatic access to NCBI databases sequence parsing and alignment.
how_to_use: Install via pip: pip install biopython. Use SeqIO to parse FASTA/GenBank files. Access NCBI databases programmatically with Entrez — fetch sequences download literature. Use the Blast module to run BLAST searches from Python scripts. Biopython integrates well with pandas and matplotlib for building reproducible analysis pipelines.

name: SBOLCanvas
description: Browser-based tool for drawing genetic circuit diagrams using SBOL Visual notation. Creates publication-ready figures.
how_to_use: Open SBOLCanvas in your browser — no installation needed. Drag and drop genetic parts (promoters RBS CDS terminators) from the parts palette. Connect parts to build your circuit diagram. Export as SVG for scalable wiki figures or PNG for presentations. Use SBOL Visual glyphs so your diagrams follow the community standard.

name: Jalview
description: Desktop application for viewing and analyzing multiple sequence alignments. Color-coding and conservation analysis built in.
how_to_use: Download Jalview and open your Clustal or MUSCLE alignment file. Apply the ClustalX color scheme to highlight conserved residues by chemical property. Use the Conservation row to quantify conservation at each position. Export high-quality alignment figures for your wiki. Jalview's overview panel helps identify conserved domains across large alignments.

name: PyRosetta
use_case: Python interface to Rosetta protein design suite
description: Python-based access to Rosetta algorithms for protein structure prediction design and analysis.
how_to_use: Apply for a free academic license and install via conda. Use the Pose object to load PDB structures. Apply the FastRelax protocol to minimize energy after mutations. Calculate binding energy changes with InterfaceAnalyzer. PyRosetta tutorials on GitHub cover common iGEM use cases like stability engineering and binding site design.

name: MEMOTE
description: Standardized testing suite for genome-scale metabolic models. Ensures your model follows community standards before publication.
how_to_use: Install via pip: pip install memote. Run memote report snapshot model.xml to generate an HTML quality report. The score reflects how well your model passes community tests for consistency completeness and annotation. Fix flagged issues before publishing your model. MEMOTE reports are increasingly required by journals for metabolic modeling papers.

name: KBase
description: Free cloud platform for genome analysis metabolic modeling and comparative genomics. No local installation needed.
how_to_use: Create a free account at kbase.us. Upload your genome sequence and use the RAST annotation app to annotate genes automatically. Build a metabolic model with the ModelSEED app — it drafts a genome-scale model from your annotation. Run flux balance analysis directly in the browser. Share your narrative (analysis workflow) with collaborators.

name: CLC Genomics Workbench
description: Commercial platform for NGS data analysis. Used by iGEM teams with institutional access for sequencing verification and genome assembly.
how_to_use: Open your FASTQ files and run the QC tools to check read quality. Use the Map Reads to Reference tool to align reads to your expected plasmid sequence — check coverage uniformly across the construct. The Variant Detection tool identifies mutations from the reference. Export alignment statistics for your wiki documentation.

name: Trimmomatic
description: Standard tool for removing adapter sequences and low-quality reads before NGS assembly or alignment.
how_to_use: Run Trimmomatic after FastQC shows adapter contamination or low-quality tails. Command: trimmomatic PE R1.fastq R2.fastq output parameters. Set LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:36 as starting parameters. Re-run FastQC on trimmed reads to verify improvement. Always trim before assembly or alignment.

name: Antimony
description: Simple text format for writing SBML models. Used with Tellurium for concise model specification.
how_to_use: Write models in plain text: S1 -> S2; k1*S1. Load in Tellurium with te.loadAntimonyModel(). Antimony is much more readable than raw SBML XML — useful for sharing models in papers and on your wiki. The Tellurium documentation includes Antimony examples for common genetic circuit motifs.

name: colabfold
use_case: Fast AlphaFold2 predictions via Google Colab
description: Free GPU-accelerated protein structure prediction running AlphaFold2 in Google Colab. Faster than official AlphaFold servers.
how_to_use: Open the ColabFold notebook in Google Colab (link above). Paste your sequence into the sequence field. Run all cells — GPU prediction takes 5-15 minutes per sequence. Download the best-ranked model PDB file. Check the pLDDT plot — blue regions (>90) are high confidence. ColabFold is the fastest free way to get AlphaFold2 predictions.

name: IQ-TREE
description: Fast and accurate tool for building phylogenetic trees from multiple sequence alignments.
how_to_use: Run IQ-TREE on your MUSCLE or Clustal alignment: iqtree -s alignment.fasta -m TEST. The -m TEST flag automatically selects the best substitution model. Output includes a .treefile you can visualize in FigTree or iTOL. Use bootstrap values (--bb 1000) to assess branch support. Phylogenetic trees show the evolutionary relationships of your target gene homologs.

name: FigTree
description: Free desktop application for viewing and annotating phylogenetic trees from IQ-TREE or other tools.
how_to_use: Open your .treefile from IQ-TREE in FigTree. Color branches by clade to highlight different organism groups. Show bootstrap support values on branches. Export as SVG or PDF for your wiki. FigTree's node annotation feature lets you add metadata (organism name isolation source) to each tip for more informative figures.

name: Galaxy
description: Free cloud platform for running bioinformatics tools without command line. Covers QC assembly annotation and more.
how_to_use: Create a free account at usegalaxy.org. Upload your FASTQ files and build an analysis workflow by chaining tools (FastQC → Trimmomatic → SPAdes). Save workflows and share with teammates. Galaxy keeps a history of every analysis step so your work is automatically reproducible. Ideal for iGEM teams without bioinformatics experience.

name: Quartzy
description: Free platform for managing lab inventory reagent orders and equipment booking. Used by iGEM teams to track consumables.
how_to_use: Create a free lab account and add your team members. Log all reagents with lot numbers and storage locations when they arrive. Use the Order Request feature to track purchases and approvals. Set low-stock alerts for critical reagents so you don't run out mid-experiment. Quartzy integrates with supplier catalogs for quick reordering.
